newsitem.title: USA: Floods, fire, evacuation at striken N.Dakota city.
newsitem.headline: Floods, fire, evacuation at striken N.Dakota city.

text.p: The swollen Red River advanced relentlessly over this flood-stricken and fire-ravaged North Dakota city on Monday, and emergency officials warned that more disaster could lie ahead.

Hospital patients and high-risk federal prisoners joined an exodus of thousands of refugees from Grand Forks, where dark, icy floodwaters swirled waist-deep through a downtown left gutted and ghostly by fire.

Authorities widened the mandatory evacuation zone to cover 90 percent of the city's approximately 50,000 residents. Across the river in East Grand Forks, Minn., the entire population was under orders to leave.
"There's always a potential for a larger area of the city to be flooded. The river is still rising," Grand Forks Emergency Manager Jim Campbell said.

Grand Fork's tribulations began this weekend when the Red River punched through clay dikes and swept into the city. A devastating fire followed, tearing through the downtown business district as several feet of water kept firefighters from doing their job.
The last of 60 hospital patients were evacuated late on Sunday night from a threatened hospital shut down because of advancing waters which had already forced thousands of local residents to flee.
Officials also disclosed that 70 prisoners had been evacuated, including 12 high-risk federal prisoners who were taken to Devils Lake, about 90 miles (144 km) west.

Residents may not be allowed to return to their homes for more than two weeks because of the lack of services. The city's water treatment plant was flooded on Saturday, and it may be three weeks before fresh water flows again.

Stunned officials spoke of the pain of seeing their city hit not only by flood but also by a fire that destroyed at least 11 buildings in the downtown area. The blaze was first reported on Saturday afternoon but was not tamed until Sunday.

Water proved to be the biggest enemy in fighting the downtown blaze. Firefighters searched frantically through murky brown floodwaters for hydrants to which they could attach hoses, only to find no pressure in the city's water system.

Firefighters eventually gained the edge by using the floodwater itself as a weapon. In desperation, they loaded a pumper truck onto the back of a trailer, and then shot floodwaters through the pumper's turret gun. Helicopters also dumped thousands of gallons (litres) of water on the blaze.

As dawn broke on Monday, the heart of Grand Forks lay blackened and in ruins, while in residential areas floodwaters continued to pour through schools, libraries and houses of the city's once-tidy neighborhoods.

"It was hard for me to see friends' houses down there. Some of them had not only gone under water but had collapsed. The foundation obviously had given away and was laying at a 45 or 50 degree angle," Lt. Byron Sieber, Grand Forks Emergency Operations spokesman, said about one city neighborhood overpowered by the river.

About 75 miles (120 km) upstream, Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness said he was optimistic because the Red River was receding at a rate of about an inch an hour (2.5 cm/hr). The Red was measured at 38.74 feet (11.8 metres) on Monday -- down more than six inches (15 cm) from the week's crest level.
"We need to have two or three good days before we are going to breathe any easier. The dikes are tired, the people are tired," Furness said.
But the Red was still rising in Grand Forks, where officials expected it to crest at 54 feet (16.4 metres) -- 26 feet (7.9 metres) above flood stage.
